questions.prompt: Shabib asks why the posterior of a 2 km rural district spans rates from 0.06 to 0.5 bursts per km-year, while a 180 km urban district's spans 0.07 to 0.10, although both used the same prior and five years of data. What is the reason?
options: The rural district's few bursts give a flat likelihood, so the prior shapes much of its posterior
The rural district's prior was wider because it is rural
The sampler mixed worse for the rural district
Rural rates are more variable by nature, whatever the data say
questions.explanation: Exposure of 10 km-years holds a handful of bursts, which constrains the rate weakly; 900 km-years constrain it sharply.
misconceptions: Thinks different widths require different priors, when the same prior was used
Blames the computation for what is a property of the data
Confuses uncertainty about a rate with variability of the process

questions.prompt: You simulate a year of bursts for a district with a rate of 0.2 bursts per km-year and 15 km of mains. Which line simulates one year?
options: rng.poisson(0.2)
rng.poisson(0.2 * 15)
rng.poisson(0.2) * 15
rng.normal(0.2 * 15, 1)
questions.explanation: The expected count is the rate times the exposure, 3 bursts, and the count is a Poisson draw with that mean.
misconceptions: Forgets the exposure: the rate is per kilometre
Scales a count drawn for one kilometre, which gives only multiples of 15
Uses a continuous distribution for a count that cannot be negative or fractional

questions.prompt: A contractor uses Normal(0, 10) on the log burst rate "to let the data speak". Its prior predictive simulation puts 37% of district-years above 500 bursts. What do you conclude?
options: The prior is harmless because the data will overwhelm it
The prior should be widened further to be safe
The prior is informative in an absurd direction and should be replaced by one that rules out impossible rates
The simulation is wrong because priors cannot predict data
questions.explanation: A prior that predicts impossible data carries strong, wrong information; with little data, as in small districts, it moves the posterior.
misconceptions: Assumes data always dominate, which fails for districts with few bursts
Believes wider is always more neutral
Does not know that a prior and a likelihood together imply a distribution of data

questions.prompt: Which reason for the prior α ~ Normal(log 0.1, 1) on the log burst rate meets the course's standard?
options: It is weakly informative
It is the default of the library
It is centred on the engineers' one burst per 10 km a year, and 73% of the network totals it simulates fall in their plausible range of 300 to 3,000
It gave the best fit to the five years of counts
questions.explanation: A reason quotes the knowledge the prior encodes and a check of what it predicts.
misconceptions: Gives a label in place of a reason
Defers to software defaults that know nothing of pipes
Tunes the prior to the same data the model will fit, using the data twice

questions.prompt: Why can Hamiltonian Monte Carlo explore a posterior with 150 parameters where a random-walk sampler stalls?
options: It evaluates the posterior on a fine grid
It uses the gradient of the log posterior to make long moves that stay in regions of high density
It discards most draws so that the rest are independent
It assumes the posterior is normal
questions.explanation: Momentum and the gradient carry the sampler far in one iteration along the shape of the posterior, so proposals are accepted often even in many dimensions.
misconceptions: Confuses sampling with grid evaluation, which is impossible in 150 dimensions
Mistakes thinning for what makes a sampler efficient
Confuses HMC with a normal approximation

questions.prompt: In log E[bursts] = log km + α + Xβ, the coefficient of log km is fixed at 1, so exp(β) for asbestos cement is a ratio of burst rates per kilometre-year.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With the offset, the other terms model the rate per unit of exposure.
misconceptions: Thinks the material coefficient compares total counts, which would mix material with network length

questions.prompt: A fit of four chains shows no divergences, bulk ESS of 7 for α and R-hat of 1.60. Three chains have a mean α near -2.41 and the fourth near -1.23. What do you do?
options: Report the pooled mean of the four chains
Drop the fourth chain and report the other three
Treat the fit as untrustworthy, rerun four chains with full warm-up from dispersed starts, and check again
Accept it, since there are no divergences
questions.explanation: Chains that disagree have not converged to one distribution; only a fresh run that passes the checks can be read.
misconceptions: Averages over chains that sample different things
Discards evidence of a problem without knowing which chains are right
Treats the absence of divergences as proof of convergence

questions.prompt: Zaina's fit hit the maximum tree depth in a third of its draws, with R-hat 1.002, bulk ESS above 1,400 and no divergences. Juhaina asks whether the numbers can be used. What do you answer?
options: Yes: capped trees cost sampling time, and the mixing diagnostics show the draws are sound
No: any warning invalidates a fit
No: the tree depth must never be capped
Only after converting the fit to a variational approximation
questions.explanation: Tree depth is an efficiency diagnostic; validity is judged by R-hat, ESS, divergences and E-BFMI, which all pass.
misconceptions: Treats every warning as a validity failure
Confuses a slow setting with a wrong one
Thinks an approximation is more reliable than a sound sampler
